opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's an interesting question, because the stereotype is that China works much harder, with "996" culture, while Silicon Valley is more relaxed. In the AI field right now, I don't think that's really true anymore.

In the last couple of years, especially since large models took off, the intensity in Silicon Valley has gone up a lot. A lot of people I know, at the big labs and at startups, work very long hours, often late into the night and on weekends. Nobody forces them. There's no official 996 policy. It's more that everyone feels this is a once-in-a-generation moment. The field moves so fast that if you take a few weeks off, a new paper or model comes out and the landscape has shifted. So there's a strong internal drive, a kind of excitement mixed with anxiety.

In my own area, robotics, it's similar. We're at a point where people believe robot foundation models might finally make general-purpose robots possible. That belief makes people willing to push very hard. You run experiments on real robots, collect data, train, evaluate, and the loop never really stops.

Compared with China, my impression is that the hours might be comparable at the top teams. The difference is more in the style. In Silicon Valley there's a bit more flexibility. People choose when and how they work, and there's more tolerance for long-term, exploratory bets that may not pay off soon. In China, from what I hear from friends and collaborators, the execution speed is incredible. Teams can iterate on hardware and products extremely quickly, and the supply chain advantage for robotics is huge. There's also more competitive pressure from many companies going after the same direction at once.

So I'd say both sides are working very intensely now. The motivation in Silicon Valley tends to come from wanting to be the one who cracks a fundamental problem. In China it's often about moving fastest and scaling first. Honestly, I think both are healthy for the field, and the competition pushes everyone forward.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and honestly my answer has shifted over the past couple of years.

For a long time the stereotype was that China was the "996" place and Silicon Valley was where people worked hard but still went home for dinner, took their sabbaticals, did their weekend hikes. I don't think that picture holds anymore, at least not in the frontier AI labs. Since the ChatGPT moment, the intensity in the Bay Area has gone up dramatically. People at the big labs are in the office late, they're on Slack on weekends, there's a real sense that every month matters because the field is moving so fast. I've had friends describe it as the most intense period of their careers, and these are people who went through earlier startup grinds.

What's interesting to me is that the intensity comes from a different place. In China a lot of the pressure is structural, it's expected by the company, it's part of the culture, and sometimes it's measured in hours rather than output. In the Valley right now it's more self-driven. People feel like they are in the middle of something historic. They want to be the one who gets the next result. Nobody is clocking you, but you also don't want to be the person who went home while your teammate made the breakthrough. That kind of pressure is harder to put down because it's internal.

The other difference is the talent density and compensation. The top labs are paying extraordinarily well, and they can afford to be selective, so you end up with a small number of extremely capable people working very hard, rather than a large headcount working long hours. Chinese labs have caught up a lot on capability, and I think the gap in raw effort has basically closed. If anything, some of the Chinese teams I've talked to are more efficient simply because they have less compute and have to be smarter about every experiment.

So my short answer: I don't think Silicon Valley is more relaxed anymore. The two ecosystems are converging in intensity. The real question is whether this pace is sustainable for either side, and I'm genuinely not sure it is.

r002.rationale: It describes late office hours and weekend Slack use in Silicon Valley, but does not characterize 70–80 hours per week as currently normal.

astra-6.text:
I think the intensity is high in both places, but it can take different forms. In Silicon Valley AI circles, a lot of the pressure comes from how quickly the field moves. You have an idea, and you feel you need to test it immediately because someone else may be working on the same thing. Even when you leave the office, it can be hard to switch off mentally.

In China, long working hours can be a more explicit expectation, although that varies a lot by company and team. I’d hesitate to say one side universally works harder. A small AI startup in Silicon Valley may be more intense than a large company in China, and vice versa.

The distinction I’d make is between hours and productive intensity. Research needs sustained effort, but it also needs room to think, to try something that fails, and to reconsider your assumptions. A packed schedule doesn’t necessarily produce better ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the intensity is high in both places, but it takes different forms. In Silicon Valley AI teams, a lot of the pressure comes from how quickly the field moves. You’re constantly asking whether an experiment worked, what you learned, and whether your direction still makes sense. That uncertainty can be exhausting even when the working hours look flexible.

In China, there’s often more emphasis on long hours and a fast execution pace. But I’d be careful about making a blanket comparison—there are big differences between companies and even between teams. For me, the important question is whether that intensity produces useful learning. Working longer isn’t automatically the same as making faster progress.
